clue.text: Illusory  happiness  of  asses approaching animal park

blocks.note: asses are silly people, fools
an old sense of paradise is an enclosed park where animals are kept

explanation.surface: Donkeys trotting up to a safari park, blissfully unaware of anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Approaching' puts the asses just before the park. The apostrophe in FOOL'S is ignored, as punctuation always is in grid entries.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a state of contentment that rests on ignorance or false beliefs, which is happiness based on illusion.

clue.text: Interval before writer becomes infiltrator

blocks.note: a fifth is a musical interval
a columnist writes a regular newspaper piece

explanation.surface: After a break, a writer turns into a spy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Interval' suggests a pause, but here it is the musical gap between notes.
explanation.definitionFit: A fifth columnist is a hidden sympathiser working against their own side from within, an enemy agent inside.

clue.text: Your, and my, party held in such regard

indicators.note: what is held in something sits inside it

blocks.note: belonging to you and me together
a do is a party

explanation.surface: Our party is so well thought of.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is used in the sense found in the phrase 'in good odour', meaning in favour with someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Odour can mean repute or esteem, as in being in bad odour with someone, so it fits regard.

clue.text: Amphibian's adaptation of sea-arm and land

definitions.note: the answer is the noun alone; 's is the link 'is'

indicators.note: an adaptation reworks material into a new form

blocks.note: taken as written, hyphen dropped
taken as written

explanation.surface: A frog-like creature evolves to cope with both sea inlet and shore.
explanation.walkthrough: Amphibians do adapt to land and water, which makes 'adaptation' look descriptive.
explanation.definitionFit: Salamanders are tailed amphibians related to newts, so one is an example of an amphibian.

clue.text: A new object thus to reverse olfactory deficiency

indicators.note: reversing turns the letters back to front

blocks.note: taken as written
standard abbreviation
an aim is a goal or object
so means in this way

explanation.surface: A fresh plan to cure a poor sense of smell.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the object and 'thus' are turned round, as a single unit; the opening A and N stay as they are.
explanation.definitionFit: Anosmia is the medical term for losing the sense of smell, a lack in the olfactory faculty.

clue.text: Drink we introduce if fish appears

indicators.note: to introduce something is to put it inside

blocks.note: ale is beer
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: We bring in a drink when fish is served.
explanation.walkthrough: The word once also meant a woman who ran an alehouse, which suits the drink in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The alewife is a North American herring-like fish that swims upriver to spawn.

clue.text: A household article in the news

blocks.note: first meaning: a couple living together
second meaning: a single story in a bulletin or paper

explanation.walkthrough: 'Household article' reads as one phrase for a domestic object, but the split falls after 'household': a couple who live together are 'an item'.
explanation.definitionFit: A romantic couple are called an item, and a single story in a newspaper or broadcast is a news item.

clue.text: Tiro ideal to become leader

indicators.note: becoming something else means changing shape into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A beginner is the perfect person to take charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leader' suggests a person, but in a British newspaper the leader is the main opinion article. A tiro is a novice.
explanation.definitionFit: The editorial, the paper's own opinion column, is called the leader or leading article in British usage.

clue.text: The average person has a way to accommodate him

blocks.note: surface reading: an ordinary member of the public

blocks.clueFragment: has a way to accommodate him
blocks.note: setter's reading: a road holds a fellow, so the phrase describes a chap placed on a thoroughfare

explanation.walkthrough: Read literally the phrase names a fellow standing on a road, so a road does indeed accommodate him.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom refers to the ordinary citizen whose views represent typical public opinion.

clue.text: Eager to travel a small distance free

blocks.note: a foot is a short unit of length
free and loose both mean not tied down

explanation.surface: Someone keen to roam, if only a short way, now that they are at liberty.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone footloose has no ties and is free to wander, so the word suits a person itching to go places.

clue.text: Girl misses end of scherzo from symphony

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, the only one kept here
something that misses a piece goes without it, so a letter drops out

blocks.note: the final letter of the musical term
the Eroica is Beethoven's Third Symphony

explanation.surface: A girl at a concert skips the last part of the lively movement in a symphony.
explanation.walkthrough: The removed letter is taken from inside the symphony's name, EROICA, leaving ERICA. 'Misses' tempts as a title for the girl, but here it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Erica is a female first name, and any girl's name can be clued simply by the word girl.

clue.text: Injury restricting Oriental wives and concubines

indicators.note: to restrict is to hem in, so one word closes round the other

blocks.note: injury and harm are synonyms
E for East, the Orient

explanation.surface: An injury that keeps eastern wives and mistresses confined.
explanation.walkthrough: E (East) sits inside HARM to make HAREM.
explanation.definitionFit: A harem is the group of women attached to one man in a traditional Muslim household, wives and concubines together.

clue.text: Island without a single channel for distributing water

indicators.note: in its older sense without means outside, so the island surrounds the other letter

blocks.note: the Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An island that has not one channel to carry water around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' reads as lacking, but it means outside: MAN goes round I. The Isle of Man is a self-governing island between Britain and Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: A water main is the principal pipe or conduit carrying the supply through a district.

clue.text: Meeting-points for first of ramblers leaving Channel Islands

indicators.note: the first of a word is just its opening letter
a letter that is leaving departs from the word it was in

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of the walkers
CI is the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Gathering places for walkers on the first leg of a trip away from Jersey and Guernsey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' is not a link here: it is the word the rambler's initial leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Foci is the plural of focus, a point where lines or rays converge, so they are points where things meet.

clue.text: Go and allow workmen finally to enter plant

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the preceding word
a letter that enters goes inside another word

blocks.note: go and pep both mean vigour
to permit is to allow
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Let the labourers finally get into the factory and start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' tempts as a factory beside the workmen, but it is the herb.
explanation.definitionFit: Peppermint is an aromatic herb of the mint family grown for its oil, so it is a plant.

clue.text: Pole enters occupied territory in pursuit of gold fabric

indicators.note: something that enters goes inside another word
what is in pursuit comes behind, so this part follows the other

blocks.note: or is gold in heraldry
the Gaza Strip, occupied by Israel in 1992
N for the North Pole

explanation.surface: A Polish soldier marches into occupied land chasing treasure, then a cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' looks like a person from Poland but means a magnetic pole. Gold as OR is a heraldic term.
explanation.definitionFit: Organza is a thin stiff sheer cloth made of silk or synthetic yarn, used for evening dresses.

clue.text: Curry never served up inside the actors' retreat

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from the bottom, so backwards
one word placed inside another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: to curry a horse is to groom it with a comb
ne'er, the poetic contraction

explanation.surface: A spicy dish never offered in the performers' lounge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curry' looks like food but is the verb for combing a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: The green room is the backstage lounge where performers wait and relax when not on stage.

clue.text: Mournful songwriter for English stage is at wit's end

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter alone

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
a leg is a stage of a journey or race
taken as written
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A gloomy composer for the London theatre has run out of ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At wit's end' is a stock phrase for desperate, but here 'at' is a link and the end of wit's gives T.
explanation.definitionFit: An elegist writes elegies, sorrowful poems or songs of lament for the dead.

clue.text: Vain American recognized by the French in their art

indicators.note: one word placed in another is surrounded by it

blocks.note: US is short for American
es is French for 'art', as in 'tu es', thou art
les is the French plural article

explanation.surface: A conceited American is acknowledged by the French for his painting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Art' is not painting: it is the old second-person form of 'to be', as in 'thou art', taken here in French.
explanation.definitionFit: Vain in the sense of futile or to no purpose, as in a vain attempt, means the same as useless.

clue.text: Elaborate clasp on the Spanish knife

indicators.note: to elaborate is to work something up into a new form

blocks.note: taken as written
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: An ornate buckle on a blade from Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: A scalpel is a small very sharp knife used by surgeons.

clue.text: Drive back, giving soldiers a beating

blocks.note: the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
a pulse is the beating of the heart

explanation.surface: An army repels attackers, giving the enemy troops a thrashing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A beating' suggests a defeat, but it is the steady beat felt at the wrist.
explanation.definitionFit: To repulse an attack is to force the attackers to retreat, the same as driving them back.

clue.text: Illegally manipulating the shrouds and stays

blocks.note: first meaning: fixing a vote or result dishonestly
second meaning: a sailing ship's ropes supporting the masts

explanation.walkthrough: Shrouds and stays sound like burial cloths and corsets, but both are ropes on a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the present participle for fraudulent fixing, and a noun for a vessel's system of ropes and chains.

clue.text: In conversation sister takes no part

indicators.note: in conversation words are spoken, so we go by their sound

blocks.note: a nun is a religious sister

explanation.surface: A sister stays silent and stays out of the discussion.
explanation.definitionFit: None means not any, so having none of something is having no part or share of it.

clue.text: Strike report

blocks.note: first meaning: to hit something hard
second meaning: the loud noise of a gun

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a news item about industrial action; 'report' is the sound of a gunshot.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for a sharp blow and a noun for an explosive noise such as a gun's report.

clue.text: Raid · the scriptures for the automation

definitions.note: a misprint for automaton, a self-operating machine

blocks.note: to raid a place is to rob it
OT, the Old Testament

explanation.surface: Looting the holy books for the sake of a machine.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed 'automation' should be 'automaton'; the answer is the machine, not the process.
explanation.definitionFit: A robot is a machine that carries out tasks by itself, which is what an automaton is.

clue.text: Fish is excellent for some!

blocks.note: first meaning: a flatfish related to the turbot
second meaning: a slang word of praise

explanation.walkthrough: 'For some!' flags that the second meaning is slang that only some people use; in Britain brill is short for brilliant.
explanation.definitionFit: Brill is a European flatfish, and in British slang a clipped form of brilliant meaning great.

clue.text: Leading character in the Roman Empire

definitions.text: Leading character in the Roman Empire

blocks.note: surface reading: a first letter, or a key figure in a story
setter's reading: one of the emperors who ruled from Rome

explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading character' invites a search for a first letter, but it simply means a ruler, the notorious emperor of the first century.
explanation.definitionFit: Nero was emperor of Rome from AD 54 to 68, so he was literally the leading figure of the empire.

clue.text: Printed music - the true facts

blocks.note: first meaning: the written copy of a composition
second meaning: the real state of affairs, as in 'know the ...'

explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes the facts sound like a gloss on the music; they are an unrelated idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical score is the notated parts of a work, and 'what's the score?' asks for the real situation.

clue.text: Formal appeal I have found in a Grandma Moses painting

blocks.note: prim means stiffly proper
it is old slang for sex appeal
the contraction I've

explanation.surface: A stiff legal plea that I have discovered in a picture by the folk artist.
explanation.walkthrough: Grandma Moses was an American self-taught painter of rural scenes. 'Formal appeal' looks like a petition but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Naive self-taught art like hers is called primitive, and one such picture can itself be called a primitive.

clue.text: Hasty departure of idle and frivolous student involved in attack

indicators.note: something involved in another is caught up inside it

blocks.note: to moon about is to idle
light-minded, not serious
a fit, as of coughing, is an attack
L for learner

explanation.surface: A lazy, flighty student in the middle of an assault hurriedly leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: L goes inside FIT to make FLIT. A moonlight flit is British slang for leaving home secretly at night to dodge the rent.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means a secret night-time removal to escape debts, a hurried exit by definition.
